The question of whether hypnosis can allow people to recall forgotten memories is genuinely contested. The majority of scientific and institutional sources argue against it: [d4] states that "nearly all the evidence suggests that hypnosis fails to aid recall, but instead has the potentially harmful effect of increasing people's faith in their memories, whether or not they are accurate recollections of events." [d8] similarly concludes that "there is no scientific evidence that hypnosis can improve the retrieval of poorly encoded memories," and warns that hypnotic suggestions may promote confabulation that neither therapist nor patient can distinguish from accurate recall. [d7], citing the American Medical Association, notes that "recollections obtained during hypnosis can involve confabulations and pseudomemories and appear to be less reliable than nonhypnotic recall," with some subjects being highly vulnerable to suggestion of false memories. [d2] adds that "recall during hypnosis can actually result in the creation of more false memories than recall while not under hypnosis," and that people tend to believe hypnotically recalled memories are accurate regardless of whether they are true. [d3] reinforces this, stating that techniques including hypnosis used in recovered memory therapy "are much more likely to distort memory than to enhance recall." On the other side, [d6] claims hypnosis "can help access the subconscious mind and retrieve forgotten memories," and [d5] cites a practicing hypnotist who estimates "a 50 to 80 percent shot at recovering a lost memory," though [d5] also acknowledges significant scientific controversy about hypnosis's validity. In sum, while some practitioners and sources assert hypnosis can unlock forgotten memories, the prevailing scientific and institutional evidence suggests it does not reliably improve recall and may instead produce false or distorted memories.
